title: Combining quality checks into three distinct end-to-end workflows
text: Part one laid out five packages. This is how they combine three endto-end workflows. What matters is not the steps, but what separates them. Three workflows. A prevents B describes. C organizes what B described. They are not three versions of the same thing and not a menu to pick one from. Workflow A. The

title: Workflow A: Preventing wrong file sizes inside the local toolkit - Workflow B: Scheduled fast metadata checks and frame-sampling downloads
text: Fellow pastes the starter block, builds as normal, and renders. The toolkit checks the size it is about to write and if it is not one of the two approved sizes, it stops and says what is wrong. Nothing is saved. They fix it, rerender, run the selfch check and upload. Workflow B runs on a schedule and touches nothing. It lists every file from the drive's own record. So the whole folder is read in seconds without downloading anything. Fellow format and resolution come from the file name. The fast checks run first and anything failing there goes no further. Only what passes gets downloaded for the slower frame check. Workflow C. Every step of B runs first, so the verdicts are settled before anything moves. Files go into two

title: Workflow C: Auto-organizing drive files and notifying submitters - Why pre-checks save upload cycles before final YouTube 4K processing
text: Folders made by hand in advance. A note sits beside each failing file with the corrected value. The fellow is sent that same line and every move is logged. What separates them? A never creates the wrong file so nothing downstream sees it. B changes nothing and prevents nothing. It exists so that no one has to open a video to find out whether it is usable. C is the only one that writes and it adds no information B did not already have. So the order is the argument. A sits up stream of B. C only makes sense once B is trusted. Someone could run all three or only B or only A. What they should not do is treat them as three bids for the same job. One thing to state plainly, our own submission guidance says the definitive 4K check happens on YouTube after processing because a local file cannot prove how YouTube will handle it. None of this removes that. What it removes is the upload cycle spent on videos that were never going to pass. Your turn. If you run this review, the question is which of the three you would trust first and whether you would rather be told earlier or told less often.
